strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: While existing domain-specific code benchmarks evaluate models on pre-existing knowledge or context-local completion, this work addresses the critical problem of evaluating how models acquire and apply external domain knowledge from paired corpora (framework documentation, source code, and examples).

Rigorous and multi-level benchmark construction: The benchmark encompasses 6 emerging domains, 11 frameworks, and 25 projects, featuring multi-granularity requirement specifications and execution-based validation with 978 unit/integration tests running in sandboxed Docker environments.

Extensive experimental evaluation: The paper conducts comprehensive evaluations across 10 modern open- and closed-source LLMs, multiple domain specialization paradigms (SFT, LoRA, BM25/Dense RAG, kNN-LM variants, synthesized instruction tuning), and autonomous coding agents (Claude Code, SWE-Agent, OpenHands).

Valuable empirical findings: The analysis provides actionable software engineering and NLP insights, notably regarding catastrophic forgetting across distant software domains during continual training, the negative/diminishing scaling trend for full-context SFT/LoRA on large code corpora, and systematic error breakdowns (e.g., API hallucinations vs. data constraint mismatches).
weaknesses: Relatively modest evaluation sample size: While curating paired corpora is labor-intensive, the final test set comprises only 131 core functions and 107 Q&A items across 6 domains. Breaking down results by domain leaves a small number of instances per cell (e.g., the RAG domain has few functions, making percentage metrics sensitive to single-item variations).

Asymmetric task coverage across domains: Code generation tasks cover only 4 of the 6 domains (RL, Agent, RAG, Model Optimization), while Embodied AI and Ascend Ecosystem only feature Q&A tasks. This creates an uneven evaluation structure where certain domains cannot be tested end-to-end on practical code synthesis.

Potential bias and lack of inter-annotator statistics in agent-assisted data creation: The benchmark relies heavily on an LLM agent (Claude Code) for requirement clarification, test generation, and Q&A drafting before human verification. The paper lacks quantitative details regarding human intervention rates, inter-annotator agreement, or verification of test suite independence, which is particularly relevant since Claude Code is also evaluated as a baseline system.

strengths: Compelling benchmark formulation: Rather than testing existing pre-trained knowledge or short-context snippet completion, the benchmark explicitly pairs curated framework knowledge corpora (source code, documentation, examples) with downstream project generation tasks, filling an important gap in evaluating domain specialization techniques for code.

Rigorous benchmark construction and execution-based validation: The annotation pipeline includes multi-agent requirement clarification, human verification, unit/integration test suites validated with coverage tools, and fully containerized Docker execution environments.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Evaluates 10 LLMs, multiple adaptation paradigms (SFT, LoRA, RAG, kNN-LM, code-specific adapters like kNM-LM and DSCC), and full coding agents (SWE-Agent, OpenHands, Claude Code).

Insightful analysis and diagnostic findings: Provides actionable empirical insights, including the inverse scaling phenomenon of corpus size for SFT/LoRA, cross-domain catastrophic forgetting, API hallucination failure modes, and agent efficiency/cost trade-offs.

Thorough appendix and robustness checks: Includes data contamination detection (CDD index), controlled agent baseline experiments matching base models, sequence length ablations, and Pass@any evaluations.
weaknesses: Modest benchmark sample size: The domain code generation task encompasses 131 core functions across 25 projects, and the understanding task has 107 multiple-choice questions. While the labor-intensive nature of verification is understandable, the relatively small number of test items per domain (around 30 functions per domain) could lead to high variance in domain-level Pass@1 metrics.

Task-domain asymmetry: Domain Code Generation only covers 4 domains (RL, Agent, RAG, Model Optimization), while Domain Knowledge Understanding covers the remaining 2 domains (Embodied AI, Ascend Ecosystem). Evaluating both understanding and generation across all domains would make the benchmark significantly more cohesive.

Limited quantitative project-level evaluation: Although the paper highlights multi-granularity evaluation from function-level to project-level, the project-level code generation benchmark is only evaluated via a qualitative case study on a single framework (VeRL in Appendix B), leaving quantitative benchmarking concentrated primarily on core functions.
Minor release / formatting omissions: The abstract contains an unpopulated repository URL placeholder ('advance further research at .').

strengths: Novel and well-motivated benchmarking paradigm: While existing code benchmarks predominantly evaluate intrinsic pre-trained knowledge or local context retrieval, KoCo-Bench explicitly pairs curated domain knowledge corpora (documentation, source code, and usage examples) with downstream target projects, enabling systematic evaluation of domain specialization methods (SFT, RAG, kNN-LM, and agents).

Rigorous execution-based evaluation: The benchmark avoids unreliable LLM-as-a-judge or surface textual overlap metrics. Domain code generation is verified via 978 unit and integration tests executed in isolated Docker containers, while domain understanding utilizes verifiable multiple-choice questions.

Comprehensive empirical scope: The paper evaluates 10 foundation models, multiple adaptation strategies (SFT, LoRA, BM25/Dense RAG, kNN-LM, DSCC), and multi-turn agent frameworks (SWE-Agent, OpenHands, Claude Code), offering valuable practical benchmarks.

Insightful downstream analyses: The studies on corpus size scaling (revealing counterintuitive negative scaling for NTP-based fine-tuning), cross-domain catastrophic forgetting, and fine-grained error taxonomy (e.g., API hallucinations and temporal/granularity data constraint mismatches) provide actionable takeaways for the code LLM community.
weaknesses: Relatively modest evaluation sample size: The benchmark contains 131 core functions across 25 projects (~5 functions per project) and 107 QA pairs. Given the small number of test instances per domain/framework, small variations in absolute solved instances can cause noticeable percentage swings in Pass@1, potentially limiting statistical significance.

Potential under-optimization of the training baselines: The primary SFT and LoRA implementations in the main text train via Next-Token Prediction on concatenated raw documentation and source files. Standard NTP continual pre-training on instruction-tuned models is known to suffer from distribution shifts and catastrophic forgetting; while Appendix D partially explores instruction synthesis, the core conclusions regarding the failure of fine-tuning may partially reflect the limitations of the training format rather than the paradigm itself.

Confounding factors in agent comparison: In the main benchmark (Table 5), Claude Code operates with Claude-Sonnet-4-5 and consumes an average of ~620k tokens per instance, compared to ~26k tokens for open-source agents powered by Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. Although Appendix G controls for the base model, token search budgets and turn dynamics remain unbalanced, complicating direct comparisons of agent architectures.

Incomplete URLs / formatting placeholders: In the abstract and Section 1, repository and resource release URLs are left incomplete (e.g., 'at .'), which should be cleaned up for the final camera-ready version.
